newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - BOLSWESSANEN PROFITS FALL, SEES RECOVERY.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BOLSWESSANEN PROFITS FALL, SEES RECOVERY.

text.p: Dutch food and drinks group Koninklijke BolsWessanen on Thursday reported a nine percent drop in 1996 net profits, but said the downward trend in its results had ended and profits from 1997 should be higher.
Net profit from ordinary operations declined 9.2 percent in 1996 to 184.2 million guilders, from 202.9 million in 1995.

After a 19.9 million guilder extraordinary charge, largely accounted for by restructurings, 1996 total net profit was 164.3 million, down from 205.8 million in 1995. The dividend was maintained at 1.28 guilders per common share.
The company had previously forecast its full-year net profit from ordinary operations would decline by 10 percent over 1996. In 1995, profits slumped 20 percent.
However, BolsWessanen said the downward trend in its results had ended in the second part of 1996 and it saw fundamental signs of recovery in profits.

"We expect from now on again a consistently positive development of our results," chairman Mac Zondervan told a news conference. "But at the same time, we want to prevent expectations from getting too high or spectacular."
Improvement would start in 1997, the company said.
"For all four product groups the 1997 operating result is expected to be higher than in 1996," it said in a statement.
"The executive board expects that, in the absence of unforeseen circumstances, net income per share from ordinary activities in 1997 will increase," it added.

The results were greeted positively by investors. At 1430 GMT, BolsWessanen shares stood up 0.90 guilders at 35.80 in a generally higher Amsterdam market. The shares earlier neared a high of 37.80 set before the 1995 results more than a year ago.
Restructurings in the firm's core businesses: dairy, convenience food and cereals, natural and speciality foods, and spirits and wines, had continued apace in 1996, Zondervan said.
The combined effect of the reorganisations would have a positive impact of at least five million guilders on net profit in 1997, he added.

For the future, BolsWessanen was targeting sales of seven billion guilders by the year 2000, Zondervan said. 1996 sales totalled 4.69 billion guilders versus 4.62 in 1995. It aimed to realise a return on sales ratio of 7.00 to 7.50 percent and a return on investment of 25 percent by the same date, he said.
Drinks firm Bols merged with food and dairy concern Wessanen in 1993, intending to use the high margins and earnings of Bols to expand in Wessanen's markets.
But the low growth potential of the group's core activities has been a major problem and it has struggled to find sizeable acquisitions in growing markets.

BolsWessanen was still looking for large acquisitions in the dairy sector, particularly in Europe, in convenience foods and in natural foods in the U.S., Zondervan said. A large buy could be financed by disposals in other areas, he said.

He denied, however, that the group's distilling activities were "in the shop window". Spirits and wines make up 15 percent of the firm's sales and have long been the focus of disposal speculation in the market.

BolsWessanen said it expects its associates' income to grow slightly in the current year, but the tax burden is expected to increase and interest charges will also rise as a result of takeovers and joint ventures which were sealed in 1996.
Capital expenditures will total 120 million guilders in 1997, slightly down from last year's 122.9 million and will be financed from the company's cash flow, it said.
